title: History and Standards

summary: A program works on Linux. What would make you confident it also works on another UNIX system?
prompt: A program works on Linux. What would make you confident it also works on another UNIX system?
explanation: Separate the API contract from one implementation. A standardized interface improves portability, but extensions, optional features and differing limits still matter.

Identify which interfaces your program relies on, then check the relevant standard and the target system's documentation. A successful build on one machine establishes very little about other systems.

title: Fundamental Concepts
reading: Read alongside Chapter 2. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: After a shell starts a program, which parts belong to the program and which belong to the kernel?
prompt: After a shell starts a program, which parts belong to the program and which belong to the kernel?
explanation: A process is a running context with memory, credentials and references to kernel-managed resources. The executable file supplies instructions; it is not the entire process.

A library call may do work entirely in user space or request a kernel service. Keeping those layers distinct helps explain why a process can replace its program yet retain its identity and some open resources.

summary: A call reports failure. Is printing a generic error enough to understand what happened?
prompt: A call reports failure. Is printing a generic error enough to understand what happened?
explanation: Read the documented return-value contract before examining errno. Many system calls report failure with -1, while other APIs use different conventions; errno alone does not tell you whether a call failed.
Capture useful error context before another call changes it. Headers describe interfaces to the compiler, while feature-test macros influence which declarations those headers expose.

concepts.title: Return values before errno
concepts.scenario: read returns zero while errno still contains an older error.
concepts.explanation: Use the return value to identify failure before interpreting errno. Zero from read can mean EOF; a previous errno value is irrelevant to that successful result.
concepts.assumptions: Read the documented result convention for each call before checking errno.
concepts.counterexample: pthread_create returns an error number directly; printing perror after it can describe an unrelated errno.

concepts.title: Headers and argument types
concepts.scenario: A compiler warns that a function is implicitly declared.
concepts.explanation: Include the documented header with feature macros defined first. Match argument types and format placeholders; a cast should express a justified conversion rather than hide an incorrect call.
concepts.assumptions: Requested feature-test macros precede all headers; function declarations must match the actual arguments.
concepts.counterexample: A program that compiles after silencing a warning may still violate the API contract at runtime.

title: File I/O: The Universal I/O Model
reference: Chapter 4 · File I/O: The Universal I/O Model · pp. 69–88
reading: Read alongside Chapter 4. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: Your copy program asks to read 4096 bytes and receives only 700. Has it reached the end?
prompt: Your copy program asks to read 4096 bytes and receives only 700. Has it reached the end?
explanation: A positive read result tells you how many bytes arrived. It may be less than requested without indicating end of file; a zero result on a regular file indicates end of file.

Treat read and write results as counts, and advance through the buffer accordingly. A file descriptor is a process-local handle, not the bytes of a file or a promise that an operation transfers everything.

concepts.title: Advance through a real buffer
concepts.scenario: read supplies 700 bytes into a 4096-byte buffer.
concepts.explanation: Only those 700 bytes are initialized by this read. Feed that actual count to a write loop and advance the pointer by the number successfully written; continue until the entire chunk is consumed.
concepts.assumptions: A byte buffer has a known capacity and each successful count advances within its bounds.
concepts.counterexample: Writing sizeof(buffer) would include bytes that were not supplied by this read.

concepts.title: Interruption and cleanup
concepts.scenario: A copy loop is interrupted while waiting for input.
concepts.explanation: Retry -1 with EINTR where the documented contract permits; handle other failures, zero progress and output errors distinctly. Keep both descriptors owned until their last use and release them on the failure path.
concepts.assumptions: The copy loop owns both descriptors; an interrupted operation may have transferred bytes if its return count says so.
concepts.counterexample: Blind retries of every error can loop forever; this regular-file copy example does not define nonblocking EAGAIN policy.

title: File I/O: Further Details
reference: Chapter 5 · File I/O: Further Details · pp. 89–112
reading: Read alongside Chapter 5. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: Two descriptors refer to one open file description. Which changes can one user see through the other?
prompt: Two descriptors refer to one open file description. Which changes can one user see through the other?
explanation: Distinguish the descriptor entry from the open file description it references. Duplicated descriptors can share a file offset and file status flags while keeping descriptor flags such as close-on-exec separate.
This distinction matters when redirecting streams or passing access to a child. Changing the shared offset can affect another descriptor even though closing one descriptor leaves the other open.

flow.title: Two entries, one open file description
flow.scope: Assume fd B is produced by dup(A), not an independent open.

nodes.label: Descriptor A: its own FD_CLOEXEC
nodes.detail: Descriptor flags belong to this entry. Changing its close-on-exec flag does not set the other entry’s flag.

nodes.label: Descriptor B: its own FD_CLOEXEC
nodes.detail: dup creates a second entry referring to the existing description; it does not independently reopen the pathname.

nodes.label: One open file description
nodes.detail: The kernel open state is shared by these two references.

nodes.label: Shared offset and status flags
nodes.detail: A read through either entry can advance this offset. O_APPEND and similar status flags belong to the description.

nodes.label: Underlying file object
nodes.detail: The file object and the per-open description are different objects.

concepts.title: dup versus open
concepts.scenario: A program creates fd2 using dup(fd1), then also opens the pathname as fd3.
concepts.explanation: fd1 and fd2 refer to one open file description and share offset/status flags. An independent successful open normally creates another description with its own offset. Descriptor flags such as FD_CLOEXEC belong to each entry.
concepts.assumptions: The duplicate comes from dup of an existing descriptor, rather than a second open.
concepts.counterexample: Equal numeric offsets observed once do not demonstrate that two descriptions are shared.

concepts.title: Positioned I/O
concepts.scenario: One component needs bytes at an explicit offset while another reads sequentially.
concepts.explanation: pread supplies a position for that operation without changing the open file description's offset. It removes one offset-coordination need, not all possible concurrent data races.
concepts.assumptions: Use a seekable regular file and explicit offsets; pread does not alter its open-file description’s current offset.
concepts.counterexample: Concurrent writers can still change the file contents or size; pread is not a snapshot or lock.

title: Processes
reading: Read alongside Chapter 6. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: Why can two running copies of the same executable have different environments and arguments?
prompt: Why can two running copies of the same executable have different environments and arguments?
explanation: Each process has its own execution context. Arguments, environment strings and memory belong to that running instance, even when the executable file is shared.
Environment variables are data supplied to a program, not a secure statement of identity. A process ID identifies a process during its lifetime; it is not a permanent name for a person or executable.

title: Memory Allocation
reading: Read alongside Chapter 7. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: A freed allocation still seems readable. Does that make using it valid?
prompt: A freed allocation still seems readable. Does that make using it valid?
explanation: Allocation lifetime is a contract of the language and allocator. Once you free an allocation, accessing it through the old pointer is invalid even when the underlying pages remain mapped.

The allocator manages blocks within a process and may reuse storage without returning pages immediately to the kernel. Separate ownership of a block from the virtual-memory mechanisms that supply its storage.

flow.title: A nonzero realloc request has two ownership outcomes
flow.scope: Assume the requested size is checked and nonzero.

concepts.title: Do not lose the original allocation
concepts.scenario: realloc fails while expanding a nonzero-sized buffer.
concepts.explanation: Store its result in a temporary pointer. On failure the original block is still owned; on success update the owning pointer. Check arithmetic before computing a new size.
concepts.assumptions: The request has nonzero size and the caller still owns the old allocation when realloc fails.
concepts.counterexample: Assigning realloc directly to the sole owner pointer can leak the old allocation on failure.

concepts.title: Mapped is not owned
concepts.scenario: A freed pointer still appears readable in a debugger.
concepts.explanation: The allocator can retain mapped pages and reuse the block. C lifetime rules still forbid accessing the released allocation, even when no page fault occurs.
concepts.assumptions: A successful mapping has a separately tracked length and lifetime; C allocation ownership is a caller discipline.
concepts.counterexample: A successful read of stale storage is not evidence that accessing it is valid or isolated from other objects.

title: Users and Groups
reading: Read alongside Chapter 8. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: A file stores a numeric owner ID. What happens if the account name changes?
prompt: A file stores a numeric owner ID. What happens if the account name changes?
explanation: User and group names are convenient mappings to numeric identifiers. File ownership and process credentials use IDs, so a renamed account can still own the same files.
Account lookups may involve configured services rather than only local text files. Handle lookup failures and avoid assuming that every numeric ID currently has a display name.

concepts.scenario: A file belongs to UID 12345 but no account lookup returns a name.
concepts.explanation: Display the numeric ID and distinguish not-found from a lookup error using the API's convention. Lookups can involve configured name services rather than only a local file.

concepts.title: Identity is not authentication
concepts.scenario: A service receives a username in a request.
concepts.explanation: Looking up that name obtains account data; it does not prove that the requester controls the account. Use the request's authenticated context for authorization decisions.
concepts.assumptions: An account lookup retrieves records; no password or authentication exchange is performed by the lookup itself.
concepts.counterexample: A name supplied in argv or an environment variable is caller-controlled input.

title: Process Credentials
reading: Read alongside Chapter 9. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: A program has a real user ID and an effective user ID. Which one explains its current access?
prompt: A program has a real user ID and an effective user ID. Which one explains its current access?
explanation: Credentials have distinct roles. Many access checks depend on effective credentials and supplementary groups, while Linux also has filesystem IDs and capability rules.
Changing identity requires attention to saved IDs, group membership and the order of operations. Do not infer that dropping one field necessarily removes every route back to privilege.

concepts.title: Inspect the complete credential set
concepts.scenario: A helper prints its real, effective and saved user IDs.
concepts.explanation: The real ID relates to process ownership history, the effective ID to many checks and the saved ID to allowed transitions. Supplementary groups and Linux filesystem IDs add authority dimensions.
concepts.assumptions: Inspect Linux real, effective, saved and filesystem IDs and supplementary groups in the relevant user namespace.
concepts.counterexample: Changing one printed ID does not prove all routes to privileged actions were removed.

concepts.title: Ordering a privilege change
concepts.scenario: A helper needs privileged group setup before dropping user privilege.

concepts.assumptions: The privilege-change example must check every transition and remaining capability; effective UID alone is insufficient.
concepts.counterexample: A failed group change followed by continued execution can preserve authority the program meant to discard.

title: Time
reading: Read alongside Chapter 10. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: A clock is adjusted while you measure a task. Could the measured duration become misleading?
prompt: A clock is adjusted while you measure a task. Could the measured duration become misleading?
explanation: Calendar time answers what time it is, while a monotonic clock is useful for elapsed intervals. Select the clock according to the question rather than treating all timestamps as interchangeable.
Process CPU time measures execution time consumed, not how long a person waited. A process blocked on I/O may have a long elapsed duration and little CPU time.

concepts.title: Measure two different questions
concepts.scenario: A worker sleeps for a second and then does a short computation.

concepts.explanation: Keep units in names and output. Borrow one second when the nanosecond difference is negative; do not compare timestamps from unrelated clock domains as if they share an epoch.
concepts.assumptions: Timestamp units and clock origins are identified before subtracting or converting values.
concepts.counterexample: Wall-clock timestamps are useful for human logs but clock adjustments can distort elapsed-time subtraction.

explanation: System inspection is a view of a changing system. Information under procfs can change or vanish between operations, so disappearance is an ordinary case to handle.

concepts.scenario: A PID listed under procfs vanishes before its status is opened.

concepts.counterexample: Permissions, kernel support and the precise operation still matter; merely obtaining a handle is not arbitrary authority over a process.

title: Sockets: Server Design

summary: A slow client stops reading. How can it affect unrelated clients served by the same program?
prompt: A slow client stops reading. How can it affect unrelated clients served by the same program?
explanation: Server structure determines where blocking and resource use accumulate. A sequential server can stop making progress for other clients while one connection occupies it.
Processes, threads and event loops make different tradeoffs in concurrency and shared state. Every design still needs connection limits, buffer limits and a policy for slow or failed peers.

concepts.title: Compare four execution structures
concepts.scenario: One client stops reading a large response.
concepts.explanation: A sequential server can block all work; per-process/thread designs bound blocking differently; event loops need nonblocking I/O and state machines. All designs still need connection and memory limits.
concepts.assumptions: The slow-client comparison includes finite connection and output-buffer capacity.
concepts.counterexample: Adding threads does not automatically bound the number of slow clients or queued response bytes.

concepts.title: Backpressure reaches the producer
concepts.scenario: A connection's output buffer reaches its configured cap.
concepts.explanation: Pause or reject upstream work according to an explicit policy, enforce deadlines where appropriate and resume only when capacity returns.
concepts.assumptions: Backpressure is propagated or a documented rejection policy is used instead of growing queues indefinitely.
concepts.counterexample: Unbounded buffering hides a slow consumer temporarily while growing the resource problem.

prompt: A successful send returns. Has the peer application processed the request?
explanation: Success usually means the local networking stack accepted bytes, not that the peer application consumed or committed them. Application acknowledgments are a separate protocol decision.

Partial transfers, half-close, socket options and ancillary data add distinct state transitions. Check the contract of each operation rather than treating a connected socket as an atomic request channel.

concepts.assumptions: A successful send may accept fewer bytes than requested and only establishes local acceptance.

concepts.assumptions: Application acknowledgment is an additional protocol requirement; EOF/half-close do not alone prove remote work succeeded.
concepts.counterexample: Closing both directions immediately may prevent receiving an application response; EOF is not a generic successful-transaction code.

title: Alternative I/O Models
reading: Read alongside Chapter 63. Start with the question below, then use the chapter to examine the assumptions in your answer.
summary: An event loop is told a descriptor is readable. Can its next read still require careful error handling?
prompt: An event loop is told a descriptor is readable. Can its next read still require careful error handling?
explanation: Readiness means an operation can be attempted under the interface's rules; it does not reserve data for a particular reader. Nonblocking I/O lets an event loop handle changed conditions without blocking unexpectedly.
With edge-triggered epoll, draining until EAGAIN is a key part of the usual protocol. Readiness, EOF and error conditions must all feed the application's state machine.

concepts.scenario: An edge-triggered epoll event announces input.
concepts.explanation: Use nonblocking I/O and continue until EAGAIN, handling EINTR, EOF and real errors separately. Preserve partial-message state across events.
concepts.assumptions: For edge-triggered readiness the descriptor is nonblocking and drained until EAGAIN, EOF or failure.
concepts.counterexample: Processing only one chunk can leave unread bytes without a new edge to wake the loop.

concepts.title: Level and edge are different progress contracts
concepts.scenario: A descriptor stays readable while input remains.
concepts.explanation: Level-triggered observation can report the persistent condition again; edge-triggered handling responds to transitions and needs deliberate draining/rearming semantics.
concepts.assumptions: Level-triggered readiness can recur while work remains; readiness is not a promise the next operation cannot race.
concepts.counterexample: Readiness does not reserve bytes for one consumer, so another thread can change the condition before read.

summary: How does a terminal emulator make a shell behave as if it has a terminal?
prompt: How does a terminal emulator make a shell behave as if it has a terminal?
explanation: A pseudoterminal provides a master/slave pair. The application on the slave side sees terminal semantics, while the program controlling the master exchanges the byte stream.
Setting up a login-like environment also involves sessions, a controlling terminal, window size and job control. A pty supplies terminal behavior; it does not by itself isolate the child process.
